title: NGC 2685: A Helix in the Sky
caption: The polar ring galaxy NGC 2685, imaged by the Gemini North telescope
celestial: NGC 2685 · constellation Ursa Major · about 40 million light-years away (source figure)
credit: International Gemini Observatory/NOIRLab/NSF/AURA/L. Bassino. Image processing: J. Miller (Gemini Observatory/NSF NOIRLab), M. Rodriguez (Gemini Observatory/NSF NOIRLab), & M. Zamani (NSF NOIRLab)

recognition.text: NOIRLab Image of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: This Gemini North image shows NGC 2685, also called the Helix Galaxy, about 40 million light-years away in Ursa Major. It is a peculiar lenticular galaxy of the type called a polar ring galaxy, meaning that a ring of gas, stars and dust circles it at right angles to the flat plane of the main galaxy.

Astronomers believe such crossed planes point to past galaxy interactions, mergers or the gravitational capture of material. Current research suggests NGC 2685 took on its present form when it pulled in material from another galaxy and stretched it into the ring that now encircles it. A lenticular galaxy, for reference, is a disk galaxy without prominent spiral arms.

As one of the closest known polar ring galaxies, it is among the easiest of its kind to study. Within the Shapley-Ames Catalog of Bright Galaxies it has been called the most unusual galaxy, and it appears as number 336 in Halton Arp's Atlas of Peculiar Galaxies.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (6.72 x 4.90 arcminutes) and distance (40 million light years), the frame spans roughly 78,000 × 57,000 light-years. Its light set out about 40 million years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: Taken in visible light with the Gemini Multi-Object Spectrograph on Gemini North through g, r and i filters. The colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: The long exposure gathers far more light than the eye, revealing the faint ring circling the galaxy.

explore: Gemini North forms half of the International Gemini Observatory, which NSF NOIRLab operates with funding from the U.S. National Science Foundation. The WIYN 0.9-meter Telescope at Kitt Peak National Observatory recorded another view of this galaxy in 1998.
